Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Ravi, a 44-year-old single man who had built a life as a chef in a busy downtown kitchen, still carried the war with him every day, though he never spoke of it. He had fled his home country during a period of ethnic cleansing, when soldiers in camouflaged uniforms had come to his village. He remembered the sound of heavy vehicles grinding over gravel, the shouting, the screams. He remembered his younger brother being dragged away, and Ravi, frozen behind a pile of rubble, doing nothing. He remembered the neighbor’s house burning, the paramedics who arrived too late, the smell of blood and diesel. That day became a permanent scar, but the words to describe it never formed. When he tried to tell the story during his asylum interview, his throat closed and he could only shake his head. The event lived in him as images and sounds, not as a narrative he could own.

In the months after resettling in the United States, Ravi noticed changes he could not name. He became hyperalert in grocery stores, scanning every aisle for exits before he could pick up a basket. He avoided parks and plazas—any open space where he could not see a clear route to a door or a car. When a police car passed his window, he would duck away from the glass and hold his breath. He could not bear the sight of a wound on someone else’s arm; a bandage in the kitchen would make his hands shake and his mind go blank. The hardest moment came when he was at a street festival and an ambulance screamed past. The siren pierced through him like a blade, and he had to sit down on the curb, drenched in sweat, unable to speak for ten minutes. He began to plan his life around such threats. He only walked routes that had multiple turnoffs. He never sat with his back to a door. In the restaurant, he positioned his station so he could see both the swing door to the dining room and the back exit to the alley.

His job as a chef should have been a refuge—controlled, hot, loud. But it became a minefield. The head chef sometimes wore a jacket that reminded Ravi of military fatigues; he would feel his spine stiffen and his voice soften, agreeing with everything the man said even when he disagreed. That fawn response disgusted him afterward. A line cook once dropped a knife and cut his finger; Ravi saw the blood and his mind went numb, as if he were watching a stranger in a movie. The grief that followed that shift was overwhelming. He would lock himself in the walk-in cooler and weep for his brother, for the people he had left behind. He could not explain to anyone why a small injury in a kitchen could send him into a spiral of guilt. He believed he had no right to be alive when others—his brother, the children from his village—were dead. He was certain that his soul had been permanently warped, that he would never feel whole or safe again.

Concentration became the first casualty. Recipes he had known for years started to slip; he would read an order three times and still forget a modifier. The head chef yelled at him, and Ravi nodded, terrified. He started arriving early to check every ingredient, double-checking as a way to manage the constant feeling that something terrible was about to happen. He avoided the staff lunchroom when veterans came in wearing their service caps. He never attended team outings that involved outdoor seating. The other cooks called him quiet, but they did not know that his quiet was a cage. Even casual conversations became landmines. One afternoon, a server mentioned a car accident she had seen on the highway—two crumpled cars, paramedics holding IV bags, a man lying on the asphalt. Ravi’s chest tightened as she spoke, and he had to turn away, pretending to scrub a cutting board. He could not listen to anyone talk about a crash, a fall, a disaster. The words drew pictures he could not unsee: bodies, blood, people running. He started excusing himself whenever someone began recounting an accident, claiming he needed the bathroom or a delivery check. The other staff assumed he was squeamish, but Ravi knew the truth: those stories pulled him right back to the burning house, to the paramedics arriving too late, to his brother’s voice calling his name in the dirt.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a shift two weeks ago. A delivery driver parked outside with a refrigerated truck that hummed like an ambulance engine. Ravi froze at the pass, dropped a pan, and could not pick it up. The kitchen fell silent. His hands trembled for the rest of the night, and that evening he found himself unable to leave his apartment, staring at the door. The next morning he called a clinic. He was tired of planning exits, tired of the numbness that came over him when he recalled his brother’s face, tired of the guilt that made him feel monstrous. He hoped, vaguely, that someone might help him find words for what he carried, but he was also terrified that if he opened the door to that memory, he would never be able to close it again.
